id: A Wasp Woman Visits a Black Junkie in Prison

outputs.L1:
After the explanations and regulations, he walked warily in. Black hair covered his chin, subscribing to the villainous ideal. “This cannot be real,” he thought. “This is a classical mistake; this is a cake baked with embarrassing icing. Somebody’s got, likely as not, a big fat tongue in cheek! What have I to do with a prim-and-proper-blooded lady?” Christ indeed has risen when a junkie in prison visits with a WASP woman.

“Hold your stupid face, man. Learn a little grace, man; drop the sacred shield a notch. She might have good reason, like: ‘I was in prison, and ye visited me not,’ or some such. So sweep clear anachronistic fear, fight the fog, and use no hot words.”

After the seating and the greeting, they fished for a denominator, common or uncommon, and could summon only the fact that both were human.

“Be at ease, man! Try to please, man! The lady is as lost as you.”

“You got children, ma’am?” he said aloud.

The thrust broke the dam, and their lines wiggled in the water. She offered no pills to cure his many ills, no compact sermons, but small and funny talk: “My baby began to walk... simply cannot keep his room clean...” Her chatter sparked no resurrection, and truly no shackles were shaken. But after she had taken her leave, he walked softly and, for hours, used no hot words.
outputs.L2:
Once the rules had been laid out and the necessary explanations given, he entered cautiously. His chin was hidden beneath dark facial hair, fitting the image of a villain. He could hardly believe the situation. To him, it seemed like an absurd blunder—something ridiculous disguised by awkward sweetness, perhaps an elaborate joke. Why had he been paired with such a refined, respectable white woman?

It would take a miracle worthy of Christ’s resurrection for an imprisoned drug addict and a WASP woman to meet this way. Still, he scolded himself: stop looking foolish, show some manners, lower your defenses. Perhaps she had a sincere motive—something like the biblical reproach, “I was in prison, and you did not visit me.” He told himself to cast aside outdated fears, push through the uncertainty, and avoid angry language.

After they sat down and exchanged greetings, they searched for any point of connection, ordinary or otherwise. The only thing they could find was their shared humanity. He urged himself to relax and make an effort, since she appeared just as uncomfortable as he was. Finally, he asked aloud whether she had children.

That question released the tension, and conversation began to flow. She did not bring medicine for his problems or deliver neat little religious lessons. Instead, she spoke lightly and humorously about everyday life: her baby had started walking, and someone simply could not keep his room tidy.

Their exchange produced no dramatic spiritual rebirth, nor did it literally break any chains. Yet after she left, he moved quietly and went for hours without using harsh words.
outputs.L3:
The prisoner regarded his visitor with open suspicion. Rough-looking and hardened by confinement, he could not imagine what he might have in common with the prim, carefully dressed woman seated across from him. Her composed manner seemed to belong to a world entirely separate from his own, and his first instinct was to dismiss her before she had even spoken.

Still, he restrained his prejudice and the anger that had become almost habitual. He reminded himself that she had chosen to come and that her reasons might be sincere. Perhaps she was not there to judge him or satisfy her curiosity. With that possibility in mind, he made an effort to listen.

Their conversation began awkwardly. Each polite question seemed to lead to another uncomfortable silence, and neither could find a subject that bridged the distance between their lives. For a while, the only thing they appeared to share was their humanity and the discomfort of two strangers trying to acknowledge it.

Then he asked whether she had children. The simple question changed the tone of the visit. Her reserve softened as she described the ordinary chaos of family life: minor arguments, embarrassing remarks, and household mishaps that had become funny in retrospect. One story led naturally to another, and before long, they were both smiling.

Nothing dramatic came of the meeting. The prisoner did not suddenly repent, nor did the woman discover a miraculous solution to his troubles. Yet after she left, something in him remained quieter. For several hours, his anger loosened its hold, and he moved through the prison with an unfamiliar calmness, speaking to others with a little more patience and gentleness than before.
outputs.L4:
The prisoner sat behind the scratched glass with his arms folded tightly across his chest. He had agreed to the visit only because an officer had told him that refusing it would be foolish. Visitors brought news, cigarettes sometimes, or at least a break in the dull sameness of the week. Still, when the woman entered the room, he regretted coming.

She was neat in a way that irritated him. Her pale blouse was buttoned to the throat, her hair pinned carefully behind her head, and she carried a small handbag on her lap as if she were waiting in a doctor’s office rather than sitting in a prison. She looked like one of those women who crossed the road when they saw a man like him approaching.

For several moments, neither of them spoke.

“You are Mr. Dlamini?” she asked at last.

He glanced at the number on his uniform. “That’s what they tell me.”

The woman stiffened, uncertain whether he was mocking her. “My name is Mrs. Mercer. I volunteer with the visitors’ group.”

“I know.”

“I wasn’t sure whether you had been told.”

“I was told.”

Silence returned. Around them, other prisoners leaned toward wives, brothers, and mothers, trying to fit whole lives into brief conversations. Telephones crackled. A child cried somewhere near the door.

Mrs. Mercer opened her handbag, then closed it again. “I’m afraid I haven’t done this before.”

“That makes two of us.”

The corner of her mouth moved, though she did not quite smile. “Then perhaps we shall both have to be patient.”

He studied her more carefully. She seemed older than he had first thought. Fine lines ran from her nose to her mouth, and her hands, clasped over the handbag, were tense. Her nervousness pleased him. It made him feel less like an object being inspected.

“Why do you do it?” he asked.

“Do what?”

“Come here.”

She considered the question. “I thought it might be useful.”

“To whom?”

“To someone who has no visitors.”

He gave a short laugh. “So you came to improve me?”

Her face flushed. “No. At least, I hope not.”

“That’s what people like you always hope. You bring your good manners into a place like this and think they’ll spread.”

“People like me?”

He looked pointedly at her clothes, her handbag, her pale face. “You know what I mean.”

For the first time, her expression hardened. “Perhaps I do. But you also seem to think you know what I mean before I have said it.”

He leaned back. Her answer surprised him.

Mrs. Mercer lowered her eyes. “I nearly did not come,” she admitted. “My husband said it was dangerous. My sister said it was foolish. I imagined all sorts of things.”

“All sorts of things about men like me?”

“Yes,” she said after a pause. “I suppose I did.”

Her honesty unsettled him more than denial would have. He had expected politeness, fear, or pity—anything he could despise. Instead, she had offered him an awkward truth.

He turned toward the window. Beyond the bars, a strip of sky showed above the prison wall.

“Do you have children?” she asked.

His shoulders tightened. “Why?”

“I have two. A son and a daughter.”

“Then you should be at home with them.”

“They are grown.”

“They still need you.”

She nodded slowly. “Yes. I think they do, though they would not admit it.”

He looked back at her. “How old?”

“My son is twenty-six. My daughter is twenty-three.”

“My girl is eight.”

Mrs. Mercer’s face changed—not with pity, exactly, but with attention. “What is her name?”

“Lindiwe.”

“Does she visit?”

“Her mother won’t bring her.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be. It’s better.” He said it quickly. “This isn’t a place for children.”

“No,” Mrs. Mercer agreed. “But it must be difficult not to see her.”

He shrugged. “She sends drawings.”

“What does she draw?”

“Mostly houses.” His voice softened despite himself. “Big houses with yellow roofs. There’s always a tree, even when there isn’t room for one. And everybody has long arms.”

“Perhaps so they can reach one another.”

He gave her a suspicious look, but she appeared embarrassed by her own remark.

“She draws me outside the house,” he said. “Her mother and herself are inside.”

Mrs. Mercer did not offer an explanation or a comforting phrase. She only said, “That must hurt.”

He stared at his hands. The anger he had carried into the room seemed suddenly too large and clumsy to hold.

“My son did not speak to me for nearly a year,” she said. “Nothing like your situation, of course. We quarreled. I thought I knew what was best for him, and he thought I knew nothing at all.”

“Which of you was right?”

“Both, probably. Or neither.”

This time he smiled, briefly.

They talked until the warning bell sounded. Not about his case or the reasons he was in prison. She did not ask whether he was guilty, and he did not tell her. They spoke instead about children who ignored advice, about the cost of shoes, about teachers, and about how daughters could make their fathers feel both proud and helpless. Mrs. Mercer told him that her daughter had once drawn on every wall in the passage. He told her that Lindiwe believed the moon followed their car at night.

When the officer called the end of the visit, Mrs. Mercer rose too quickly and almost dropped her handbag.

“Will you come again?” he asked.

The question escaped before he could make it sound casual.

“If you would like me to.”

He shrugged, but there was less defiance in it now. “You can if you want.”

She nodded. “Then I will.”

Nothing dramatic happened after she left. He did not become a different man. The prison walls did not seem lower, nor did he suddenly forgive the people he blamed for putting him there. He still distrusted Mrs. Mercer’s world, and perhaps she still feared parts of his.

Yet that evening, when another prisoner made a bitter joke about women like her, he did not laugh. He thought instead of her nervous hands, her stubborn honesty, and the way she had listened when he spoke of Lindiwe.

For an hour, she had not treated him as a number, a threat, or a cause. She had treated him as a father. And he, reluctantly, had seen her not as an intruder from an enemy world, but as a mother who also knew regret.

It was a small change, almost too small to name. But in a place built of iron, anger, and suspicion, even a small opening could admit a little light.
outputs.L5:
After the storm, Mara walked alone along the empty road. The pavement shimmered beneath the streetlights, and every window in the sleeping town was dark.

At the corner, she noticed a black cat watching her from beneath an old wooden bench. It followed her quietly, step after step, until she reached home.

When Mara opened the door, the cat slipped inside. For the first time that night, she no longer felt alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a narrative prose poem about a Black prisoner reluctantly meeting a prim white woman visitor, overcoming racial suspicion through ordinary conversation, and resolving to temper his angry language afterward.
counterfactuals.output:
He almost refused the visit. A white woman, the guard said, smoothing the words as if they were clean sheets. She waited beyond the wire in a blue dress buttoned to the throat, gloves folded in her lap, her pale hair pinned so tightly it seemed even sorrow could not disturb it. He entered carrying every warning his life had taught him. She rose. He did not offer his hand.

At first they spoke like people crossing ice. She asked whether the rain had reached the prison yard. He said the roof leaked over his bunk. She told him her kitchen window leaked too, always above the basil. He nearly laughed at the smallness of this, then did. She confessed she could not keep basil alive. He said his mother grew it in a chipped coffee tin and pinched the leaves gently, as though blessing a child.

From there they wandered into ordinary country: bad coffee, bus delays, the stubbornness of buttons, the radio announcer who swallowed half his words. She had brought no sermon, only a library form and a complaint about the cold. He had brought no patience, yet found some beside them on the metal table, plain as the two paper cups cooling between their hands.

When the bell rang, she stood and drew on her gloves. “I hope you’ll write,” she said, not sweetly, not fearfully, but as one person asking another to continue a sentence.

Back in his cell, anger returned; it knew the route. It struck its match against the old walls. But that night he considered his language—the words he had sharpened until they cut friend and enemy alike. He would not surrender the fire. The world had earned his fury. Still, he resolved to bank it, to make it give heat as well as smoke, to speak hard truths without making every human face a target.

He began a letter: The rain came through again. Then, after a pause: Tell me what you did wrong with the basil.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a satirical, rhyme-filled dramatic monologue inspired by the biblical line “I was in prison and ye visited me not,” portraying an awkward prison visit that produces no miracle but leaves the inmate subtly changed.
counterfactuals.output:
**Visiting Hours**

“I was in prison, and ye visited me not”—  
That verse has always sounded rather hot,  
A trumpet aimed at every pious ear:  
*Go see the chained, or judgment may be near.*

Well, Reverend Plum came Tuesday, half past three,  
With pamphlets, mints, and nervous charity.  
He wore a tie depicting Noah’s ark  
And smiled as though he’d parked somewhere too dark.

The guard said, “No embrace, no passing things.”  
Plum coughed and tucked away two angel wings—  
Cardboard, I mean, with glitter round the hem.  
“Craft night,” he sighed. “The Lord inspired them.”

We sat. The bolted table shone like doubt.  
He asked when I expected to get out.  
I said, “The state and I still disagree.”  
He laughed too loud, then blamed acoustics. “See,

The Lord,” he said, “can break the strongest chain.”  
Just then his visitor badge snapped in twain.  
He called the guard. The guard called someone worse.  
Thus bureaucracy rebutted chapter, verse.

Plum tried a hymn. He pitched it much too high;  
A camera blinked its little metal eye.  
He lowered both his voice and, by degrees,  
His claims regarding instant inner peace.

“No lions here,” I said. “No furnace flame.  
No angel knows my booking number, name.  
No earthquake comes to spring the locks at night—  
The wiring barely keeps the hallway light.”

He nodded, though his eyes inspected me  
Like bruised fruit marked *Reduced for Charity*.  
Then asked what sin had brought me to this place.  
I said, “A judge, poor luck, and lack of grace.”

He offered me a mint. The guard said, “No.”  
Plum ate it sadly. “Rules are rules, you know.”  
“Amen,” I said. “That’s gospel here, old son:  
The state writes ten commandments every one.”

He had no gift for silence, so he spoke  
Of golf, his gout, his daughter’s second bloke,  
The church roof fund, a deacon’s vanished cash—  
How saints turn wolves when budgets start to clash.

And then—no choir. No key. No thunderclap.  
No holy jailbreak drawn upon a map.  
The walls stayed walls; the bars remained employed;  
The guards stayed bored; the faithful stayed annoyed.

But when the bell announced his hour was through,  
He fumbled with his coat and dropped one shoe.  
He bent, I bent; our foreheads struck. “Good Lord!”  
He yelped. I laughed. The guard looked vaguely bored.

Plum rubbed his brow. “I’m sorry.” So was I—  
Not saved, not cleansed, not fitted for the sky,  
But sorry he must drive back through the rain  
With half a badge and twice his former pain.

He said, “I’ll come next Tuesday, if I can.”  
Not *God commands*. Not *I will save this man*.  
Just *if I can*—a frail, unpolished phrase,  
Too small for stained-glass windows, hymns, or praise.

I watched him leave, still limping from the shoe.  
No prison doors flew open as he withdrew.  
Yet all that night, beneath the buzzing light,  
I did not curse the dark with quite such spite.

So write this down, you keepers of the plot:  
I was in prison. Ye visited—what?  
No miracle. No halo. No grand art.

Just one fool at the glass.

And one less stone inside my heart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Retell a prison visitation scene in experimental free verse, using internal rhyme, unusual capitalization, racial tension, Christian imagery, and the recurring phrase “use no hot words.”
counterfactuals.output:
The guard says, **use no hot words.**

as if language were a skillet,  
as if the tongue could blister steel.

Ma enters beneath the fluorescent CROSS—  
one tube stuttering, one tube dead—  
her purse turned out like a small confession:

peppermint, comb, bus pass,  
a photograph of him at ten  
holding a fish / holding his grin  
against the bright hook of morning.

The white guard palms each thing  
with the boredom of empire.

The Black guard looks away,  
jaw tight as a locked hymn.

**use no hot words.**

Beyond the glass, Isaiah arrives  
in county orange—

not sunrise orange,  
not marigold, not flame,

but the orange of STOP / caught / bought  
by a system that calls every cage  
a correction.

Ma lifts the phone.

He lifts the phone.

Between them:  
wire, glare, the thin skin of sound.

BABY, she mouths.

MAMA, he answers,

and the words go cold through the receiver,  
go old, go almost holy.

Behind him, an officer says MOVE.  
Behind her, a woman weeps without noise,  
rocking an invisible child.

Isaiah says they keep calling him *boy.*

Ma says, Don’t—

**use no hot words.**

He says the prosecutor smiled  
when he named the street,  
said *those people,*  
said *pattern,* said *predator,*

each syllable washed white  
as Pilate’s hands.

Ma closes her eyes.

In the black chapel of her lids  
Christ hangs again—  
brown ribs, split lip,  
state-issued sorrow.

She wants to say  
HELL.  
She wants to say  
BURN.  
She wants to say the judge’s name  
until the name becomes a match.

Instead:

I planted tomatoes.

A pause.

Red ones? he asks.

Red as—

She stops.

The guard’s gaze clicks toward her.

**use no hot words.**

Red as Sunday hats, she says.  
Red as the choir when the Spirit gets in.

Isaiah laughs—half cough, half psalm—  
and for one second the room loosens:

chains become chimes,  
glass becomes water,  
the phone cord curls like a vine  
around a ruined Eden.

Then the light flickers.

TIME.

Such a little word  
for such a large theft.

Ma presses her palm to the barrier.  
Isaiah fits his palm to hers—

dark hand / dark hand,  
no touch, all touch,

a sacrament without bread,  
without wine,  
without mercy from the state.

The guard says, **use no hot words.**

So Ma whispers coolly,

I love you.

And the sentence burns  
all the way down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary poem in which a cynical incarcerated man and a well-mannered female volunteer initially struggle to find common ground, then connect by talking about their children and everyday family problems.
counterfactuals.output:
**Visiting Hours**

He met her kindness with a rusted laugh,  
leaned back beneath the humming strip of light.  
She set her careful handbag by the chair  
and called him *sir*, which made him laugh again.

“Come here to save me?”  
“No,” she said,  
smoothing the crease in her visitor’s badge.  
“I brought some books.”

He eyed the titles—gardens, hope,  
a paperback with half a sunset on it.  
“Hope’s contraband,” he said. “And flowers die.”  
She answered, “Usually from too much water.”

The silence afterward was hard and square.  
Beyond the wired glass, a guard turned keys.  
She asked about the weather; he said, “Still there.”  
He asked about her church; she said, “Still flawed.”

They might have parted strangers,  
polite as doors that never open,  
had her phone not buzzed inside her bag—  
three times, then twice, then three again.

“My daughter,” she sighed. “She’s lost her shoes.”  
“Both?”  
“Only one. The important one, apparently.”  
He smiled despite himself.

“My boy hides homework in the freezer,” he said.  
“Claims the cold keeps it from getting harder.”  
She laughed—not volunteer laughter,  
but the helpless kind that bends the head.

Then came the true small litany:  
a son who would not wash his hair,  
a daughter furious over peas,  
rent due Friday, fevers Sunday,  
permission slips unsigned,  
a birthday cake collapsed  
but eaten anyway.

He told her how his youngest  
used to sleep with one sock on,  
how through the prison phone she asked  
if he still knew her middle name.

The woman folded both hands in her lap.  
“My oldest thinks I never listen.”  
“Do you?”  
“Not enough.”  
“Me neither,” he said.

The lock clicked somewhere down the hall.  
No walls dissolved. No angel came.  
His sentence stayed a row of iron numbers;  
her manners stayed as neat as folded linen.

But between them stood a kitchen table—  
scarred, unpaid for, crowded with children—  
and for a while they sat there, passing bread,  
complaining softly of the ones they loved.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a mid-century-style social commentary poem about an interracial prison visit. Blend humor, irony, colloquial dialogue, religious allusions, and fishing imagery, ending with the prisoner walking softly and avoiding profanity for several hours.
counterfactuals.output:
### Visiting Sunday, 1956

The guard said, “Ma’am, you kin is which?”  
She pointed through the wire.  
“My kin’s the man in county blue.”  
He coughed and checked the fire.

She was pale as a Sunday glove;  
he was dark as Jordan mud.  
Between them lay a little glass  
and all the nation’s blood.

“Well, Ruth,” he said, “you catch my note?”  
“I did. Your spelling’s worse.”  
“Paul wrote good from jail,” he grinned.  
“Paul didn’t have your nurse.”

The guard laughed once, then swallowed it,  
as if a hook went down.  
Outside, the sheriff’s campaign sign  
said **JUSTICE SERVES THIS TOWN**.

She brought no pie—they searched the pie—  
no Bible with a spine,  
no silver fishhook, pocketknife,  
nor homemade Jesus wine.

“So what’d you bring?”  
“My ugly face.”  
“That ain’t allowed in here.”  
“Then half the law should be locked up.”  
The guard said, “That’s enough, dear.”

They talked of catfish under docks,  
how patience schools the wrist;  
how some men bait the world with fear  
and swear the hook don’t exist.

He said, “The Lord made every fish.”  
She said, “And every fool.”  
He nodded toward the courthouse roof:  
“Then Heaven’s overfull.”

The bell rang out. She touched the glass.  
He raised his hand to hers—  
two palms divided by a law  
that quoted Bible verses.

Then down the block he walked so soft  
the keys forgot to chime,  
and for several whole astonished hours  
he did not swear one time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
